Genesis 1.summary: Genesis opens with God creating the heaven and the earth (Genesis 1:1–2). Over six days God brings light, sky, land and plants, the sun, moon, and stars, sea creatures and birds, and land animals into an ordered, fruitful world (Genesis 1:3–25). God creates human beings, male and female, in his image, blesses them, and gives them the job of filling and caring for the earth (Genesis 1:26–30). God looks at everything he has made, "and, behold, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31). The chapter shows God as the maker of everything and gives every person worth.
Genesis 1.whereWeAre: This is the first page of the Bible. Before there are any people, places, or kings, God creates the heavens and the earth in six days. He rests on the seventh day at the start of chapter 2, which then tells the story of the first man and woman up close.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Speaks the world into being, fills it with life, and calls it good.

keyFigures.name: The first man and woman
keyFigures.role: Made in God's image and given the job of filling and caring for the earth.

keyThemes.explanation: Everything exists because God made it. No other power shares the work.
Day by day God shapes and fills the world, and each time he sees that it is good.
Both male and female are made in God's image, so every person has worth.
God gives people the task of filling the earth and ruling over its creatures with care.

explainedReferences.explanation: The creation statement about male and female.
The creation of male and female.

Genesis 2.summary: God completes his creative work and rests on the seventh day, blessing and making it holy (Genesis 2:1–3). The account then focuses on the human setting: God forms the man from dust, places him in the garden of Eden to work and keep it, and commands him not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. God brings animals before the man to be named, yet none is a corresponding partner. God forms the woman, and the man welcomes her; the narrative concludes by explaining the close bond of marriage (Genesis 2:4–25).
Genesis 2.whereWeAre: Chapter 1 told how God made the whole world in six days. Now the story slows down and zooms in on one garden, one man, and one woman. The one command God gives here, not to eat from one tree, sets up what goes wrong in chapter 3.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Rests on the seventh day, plants the garden, gives the one command, and makes the woman.

keyFigures.name: Adam
keyFigures.role: Formed from the dust, he tends the garden and names the animals.

keyFigures.name: The woman
keyFigures.role: Made from Adam's rib to be his partner. She is named Eve in chapter 3.

keyThemes.explanation: God blesses the seventh day and makes it holy. Israel's Sabbath follows this pattern.
God breathes life into the man and gives him a home. None of it is his own doing.
The man may eat from every tree but one. That one limit tests whether he will trust God.
God says it is not good for the man to be alone. Marriage joins husband and wife as "one flesh."

explainedReferences.explanation: Resting on the seventh day.
The statement that Adam became a living soul.
The words that two become one flesh.
The marriage statement about two becoming one flesh.
Leaving parents and becoming one flesh.
The statement that husband and wife become one flesh.

Genesis 3.summary: The serpent questions God’s command and persuades the woman to eat the forbidden fruit; she also gives some to the man, who eats (Genesis 3:1–7). They become aware of their nakedness and hide. God questions them, and both shift responsibility. God curses the serpent and the ground; childbirth will be painful, work will be hard, and the man will return to dust (Genesis 3:14–19). The man names his wife Eve, God clothes them, and they are sent from Eden, with cherubim guarding access to the tree of life (Genesis 3:20–24). The chapter shows how disobedience broke humanity's closeness with God and cost them life in the garden.
Genesis 3.whereWeAre: Chapter 2 ended with the man and woman in the garden, with everything they needed and one command to keep. Here they break that command, and everything changes. From this point on, Genesis shows sin spreading, starting with Cain killing his brother in chapter 4.

keyFigures.name: The serpent
keyFigures.role: A crafty creature that questions God's word and tempts the woman. Later Scripture calls Satan "that old serpent" (Revelation 12:9).

keyFigures.name: Eve
keyFigures.role: Eats the forbidden fruit and gives some to her husband.

keyFigures.name: Adam
keyFigures.role: Eats the fruit, hides from God, and blames his wife.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Questions them, tells them what their sin will bring, clothes them, and sends them out of Eden.

keyThemes.explanation: The serpent makes God's command sound unfair and his warning sound false.
Sin brings fear and blame. The man and woman hide from God and point at each other.
Pain, hard work, and death enter the world because of this choice.
Even as he sends them out of the garden, God makes clothes to cover them.

Genesis 4.summary: Eve bears Cain and Abel. Cain, a farmer, becomes angry when God regards Abel and his offering but not Cain and his; God warns Cain that sin desires to master him (Genesis 4:1–7). Cain murders Abel and is judged to a restless life, though God places a protective sign on him (Genesis 4:8–16). Cain’s descendants establish a city and develop herding, music, and metalworking; Lamech boasts of violence (Genesis 4:17–24). Adam and Eve also have Seth, and the chapter ends by mentioning Enos and the practice of calling on the LORD’s name (Genesis 4:25–26).
Genesis 4.whereWeAre: Adam and Eve now live outside the garden, and sin moves fast. In the very next generation, one brother kills another. The chapter ends with a new son, Seth, whose family line is traced in chapter 5.

keyFigures.name: Cain
keyFigures.role: Adam and Eve's firstborn, a farmer, who kills his brother in anger.

keyFigures.name: Abel
keyFigures.role: Cain's younger brother, a shepherd, whose offering God accepts.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Warns Cain, confronts him after the murder, and puts a mark on him for protection.

keyFigures.name: Lamech
keyFigures.role: One of Cain's descendants, who brags about killing a man.

keyFigures.name: Seth
keyFigures.role: Adam and Eve's third son, born to take Abel's place.

keyThemes.explanation: God accepts Abel's offering but not Cain's. Hebrews says, "By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain" (Hebrews 11:4).
God warns Cain that "sin lieth at the door" and that he must rule over it.
Abel's blood cries out to God from the ground, and Cain must answer for his brother's death.
Cain is driven away, yet God protects him from anyone who might kill him.

Genesis 5.summary: Genesis 5 traces the family line from Adam through Seth to Noah. It recalls that God made humanity in his likeness and blessed them (Genesis 5:1–2). Each generation lists years of life, sons and daughters, and death, a reminder that everyone dies. Enoch is an exception to the ordinary formula: he walks with God, and God takes him (Genesis 5:21–24). Lamech names Noah with words expressing hope for relief from painful labor (Genesis 5:28–31). The list links the first people to the flood story that comes next.
Genesis 5.whereWeAre: Chapter 4 followed Cain's family. This chapter follows Seth's line instead, ten generations from Adam to Noah. It closes with Noah and his three sons, the family at the center of the flood story in chapters 6–9.

keyFigures.name: Adam
keyFigures.role: The first man. The family list begins with him.

keyFigures.name: Seth
keyFigures.role: Adam's son, through whom this family line runs.

keyFigures.name: Enoch
keyFigures.role: Walks with God and is taken by God without dying.

keyFigures.name: Methuselah
keyFigures.role: Enoch's son, who lives 969 years, the longest life in the Bible.

keyFigures.name: Lamech
keyFigures.role: Noah's father, who hopes his son will bring comfort from hard work.

keyFigures.name: Noah
keyFigures.role: Born at the end of the list. He will be at the center of the flood story.

keyThemes.explanation: The list begins by remembering that God made humanity in his likeness and blessed them.
Again and again the list ends with "and he died." God's warning in Eden has come true.
Enoch breaks the pattern. He walks with God, and God takes him.
Lamech names his son Noah, hoping he will bring rest from the hard work of the cursed ground.

Genesis 6.summary: As humanity multiplies, Genesis tells how "the sons of God saw the daughters of men" and took them as wives, mentions the "giants in the earth," and reports the spread of human wickedness (Genesis 6:1–5). God grieves over the corruption and announces judgment, yet Noah finds favor (Genesis 6:6–8). Noah is described as righteous in his generation. God tells him that the earth is full of violence and commands him to construct an ark, preserve his family, and bring representatives of living creatures aboard (Genesis 6:9–22). The chapter moves from a world full of evil to God’s plan to save Noah’s family.
Genesis 6.whereWeAre: The world has filled with people since Adam, but it has also filled with evil. This chapter tells why God sends the flood and how he plans to save Noah's family. The flood itself begins in chapter 7.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Sees the evil on the earth, decides to send a flood, and tells Noah to build an ark.

keyFigures.name: Noah
keyFigures.role: A righteous man who walks with God and does everything God commands.

keyFigures.name: Noah's family
keyFigures.role: His wife, his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and their wives, who will be saved in the ark.

keyFigures.name: The sons of God and the giants
keyFigures.role: The "sons of God" take wives from the "daughters of men," and "giants" live on the earth in those days.

keyThemes.explanation: Every thought of the human heart has become evil, and violence fills the earth.
Human evil grieves God's heart, and he does not ignore it.
"But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD." Noah walks with God in a wicked world.
Noah builds the ark exactly as God tells him.

Genesis 7.summary: God instructs Noah to enter the ark with his household and the animals, distinguishing clean from unclean animals for the numbers taken (Genesis 7:1–5). Noah obeys; rain falls for forty days and nights, the fountains of the deep break open, and the waters rise (Genesis 7:6–20). Living creatures outside the ark perish, while Noah and those with him remain alive. The waters prevail for 150 days (Genesis 7:21–24). The chapter shows harsh judgment, and life saved by following God's instructions.
Genesis 7.whereWeAre: In chapter 6 God told Noah to build the ark, and Noah did everything he was told. Now the rain comes and covers the earth. This is the low point of the flood story; in chapter 8 the waters start to go down.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Tells Noah to enter the ark, shuts the door, and sends the flood.

keyFigures.name: Noah
keyFigures.role: Obeys God and goes into the ark with his family and the animals.

keyFigures.name: Noah's family
keyFigures.role: His wife, his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and their wives, who are kept safe in the ark.

keyThemes.explanation: Noah does all that God commands, before the first drop of rain falls.
The waters cover the whole earth, and every living thing outside the ark dies.
God keeps Noah, his family, and the animals alive through the flood.
The LORD himself shuts Noah in. Noah's safety is God's doing, not his own.

Genesis 8.summary: God remembers Noah and the creatures with him, and the waters begin to recede (Genesis 8:1–5). Noah sends out a raven and then a dove in stages to test the earth’s condition (Genesis 8:6–12). When the ground is dry, God tells Noah and his household to leave the ark with the animals (Genesis 8:13–19). Noah builds an altar and offers burnt offerings from clean animals and birds. God pledges that the regular rhythms of earth will continue and that he will not again strike down every living thing in the same way (Genesis 8:20–22).
Genesis 8.whereWeAre: The whole earth has been under water since chapter 7. Now the story turns: "God remembered Noah" (Genesis 8:1), and the waters go down. Noah's offering at the end leads into God's covenant with him in chapter 9.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Remembers Noah, dries up the waters, and promises never again to destroy every living thing.

keyFigures.name: Noah
keyFigures.role: Sends out a raven and a dove, leaves the ark when God says, and builds an altar.

keyFigures.name: Noah's family
keyFigures.role: Steps out of the ark with Noah to begin life again.

keyThemes.explanation: God has not forgotten Noah. He sends a wind, and the waters begin to go down.
Noah tests the land with birds, but he leaves the ark only when God tells him to.
Noah's first act on dry land is to build an altar and worship.
God promises that seedtime and harvest, summer and winter, and day and night will not stop.

Genesis 9.summary: God blesses Noah and his sons and tells them to multiply. They may now eat animals, but not blood, and murder is treated with special seriousness because humans bear God’s image (Genesis 9:1–7). God makes a covenant with Noah, his descendants, and living creatures never again to destroy all flesh by flood, giving the rainbow as its sign (Genesis 9:8–17). Later Noah becomes drunk, Ham sees his father’s nakedness, Shem and Japheth cover him, and Noah speaks blessings and a curse concerning Canaan (Genesis 9:18–29).
Genesis 9.whereWeAre: Noah's family has just stepped out of the ark into an empty world. God gives them a fresh start, much like his first blessing on Adam and Eve in chapter 1. The chapter ends with a family failure that leads into the list of nations in chapter 10.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Blesses Noah's family and makes a covenant with every living thing, marked by the rainbow.

keyFigures.name: Noah
keyFigures.role: Receives the covenant, plants a vineyard, and later blesses and curses his sons' families.

keyFigures.name: Shem and Japheth
keyFigures.role: Cover their father's shame without looking.

keyFigures.name: Ham
keyFigures.role: Sees his father's nakedness and tells his brothers.

keyThemes.explanation: Murder is a grave wrong because every person is made in God's image.
God promises never again to destroy the earth by a flood, and the rainbow is the sign.
God repeats his first blessing: be fruitful, multiply, and fill the earth.
Even after the flood, sin shows up in Noah's own tent.

Genesis 10.summary: After the flood, Noah's sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth have families that grow into nations (Genesis 10:1). Japheth's descendants spread out to the isles (Genesis 10:2–5). Ham's line includes Cush, Mizraim (Egypt), and Canaan, and the mighty hunter Nimrod, whose kingdom begins at Babel in the land of Shinar (Genesis 10:6–20). Shem's line runs through Eber and Peleg toward Abraham's family (Genesis 10:21–31). The chapter, often called the Table of Nations, shows humanity spreading out by families, languages, and lands (Genesis 10:32).
Genesis 10.whereWeAre: After the flood, Noah's three sons have families, and those families grow into nations. This chapter is a map of the world as Israel knew it. Chapter 11 goes back and tells how those nations were scattered at Babel.

keyFigures.name: Japheth
keyFigures.role: Noah's son whose descendants spread to the isles.

keyFigures.name: Ham
keyFigures.role: Noah's son whose line includes Cush, Egypt, and Canaan.

keyFigures.name: Nimrod
keyFigures.role: "A mighty hunter before the LORD," whose kingdom begins at Babel.

keyFigures.name: Shem
keyFigures.role: Noah's son whose line runs through Eber toward Abraham.

keyThemes.explanation: Every nation on the list comes from Noah's three sons.
The peoples spread out, each with its own land, language, and family.
Nimrod builds the first kingdom, with cities like Babel in the land of Shinar.
Shem's line is traced with care, because Abraham will come from it.

Genesis 11.summary: People sharing one language settle on a plain in Shinar and decide to build a city and tower to make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered (Genesis 11:1–4). God confuses their language, and they disperse; the place is called Babel (Genesis 11:5–9). The chapter then gives Shem’s genealogical line through Terah, introduces Abram, Nahor, and Haran, names Sarai and Milcah, notes Sarai’s childlessness, and describes Terah’s household moving from Ur toward Canaan but settling in Haran (Genesis 11:10–32).
Genesis 11.whereWeAre: The nations listed in chapter 10 all once spoke one language. This chapter shows how they were scattered at Babel. Then the story narrows to one family line, ending with Abram, the man God calls in chapter 12.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Comes down, confuses the builders' language, and scatters them.

keyFigures.name: The builders of Babel
keyFigures.role: People who try to build a tower to heaven and make a name for themselves.

keyFigures.name: Terah
keyFigures.role: Abram's father, who moves his family from Ur toward Canaan but stops at Haran.

keyFigures.name: Abram and Sarai
keyFigures.role: Introduced at the end of the chapter. Sarai has no children.

keyFigures.name: Lot
keyFigures.role: Abram's nephew, whose father Haran has died.

keyThemes.explanation: The builders want to make a name for themselves and stay together instead of filling the earth.
God stops the tower by confusing the builders' language.
The chapter explains how one people became many peoples with many languages.

keyThemes.theme: From the nations to one family
keyThemes.explanation: The family list narrows the whole story down to Abram.

Genesis 12.summary: God calls Abram to leave his land and relatives for a land God will show him, promising to make him a great nation and a blessing to all families of the earth (Genesis 12:1–3). Abram travels with Sarai and Lot to Canaan, where God promises the land to his offspring; Abram builds altars (Genesis 12:4–9). Famine drives them to Egypt. Fearing for his safety, Abram presents Sarai as his sister; Pharaoh takes her into his household, but plagues strike, and Pharaoh sends them away (Genesis 12:10–20).
Genesis 12.whereWeAre: After eleven chapters about the whole world, Genesis now focuses on one man. Abram was introduced at the end of chapter 11. Here God calls him to leave home, and the rest of Genesis follows his family.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Calls Abram to leave home and promises him land, a great nation, and a blessing for all families.

keyFigures.name: Abram
keyFigures.role: Leaves Haran at seventy-five, builds altars in Canaan, then lies about his wife in Egypt.

keyFigures.name: Sarai
keyFigures.role: Abram's wife, taken into Pharaoh's house because of Abram's lie.

keyFigures.name: Lot
keyFigures.role: Abram's nephew, who travels with him.

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh
keyFigures.role: King of Egypt, who sends Abram away after plagues strike his house.

keyThemes.explanation: Abram leaves everything familiar because God tells him to.
God's plan for Abram reaches "all families of the earth."
Wherever God appears to him, Abram builds an altar.
Afraid for his life, Abram lies about Sarai and puts her in danger.

explainedReferences.explanation: Instruction to Abraham to leave his country and family.
Promise that all families of the earth will be blessed through Abraham's seed.
Promise that the nations would be blessed through Abraham.

Genesis 13.summary: Abram returns from Egypt toward Bethel with Sarai and Lot. Their substantial flocks create conflict between their herders, so Abram offers Lot first choice of land (Genesis 13:1–9). Lot chooses the fertile Jordan plain and settles near Sodom, whose people are described as wicked (Genesis 13:10–13). God renews the promise that Abram’s descendants will receive the land and become innumerable. Abram moves near Hebron and builds an altar (Genesis 13:14–18).
Genesis 13.whereWeAre: Abram has just come back from Egypt, richer but humbled after lying about Sarai. Now he and his nephew Lot have too many animals to live together. Lot's choice of land near Sodom sets up the rescue in chapter 14 and the destruction in chapter 19.

keyFigures.name: Abram
keyFigures.role: Makes peace with Lot, lets him choose first, and receives God's promise again.

keyFigures.name: Lot
keyFigures.role: Chooses the green Jordan plain and moves toward Sodom.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Promises Abram all the land he can see and children as many as the dust.

keyFigures.name: The herdsmen
keyFigures.role: Abram's and Lot's herdsmen, whose quarrel leads to the split.

keyThemes.explanation: Abram ends the quarrel by giving Lot first choice of the land.
Lot picks the land that looks best, near the wicked city of Sodom.
Right after Lot leaves, God promises Abram all the land he can see.
Abram settles at Hebron and builds an altar.

Genesis 14.summary: A coalition of eastern kings wages war against kings of the Jordan plain, including Sodom (Genesis 14:1–12). Lot is captured, and Abram gathers trained men, pursues the raiders, and rescues Lot and the captives (Genesis 14:13–16). Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings bread and wine and blesses Abram; Abram gives him a tenth. Abram refuses the king of Sodom’s goods so that the king cannot claim to have enriched him (Genesis 14:17–24).
Genesis 14.whereWeAre: Lot moved near Sodom in chapter 13. Now war comes to those cities, and Lot is taken captive. After Abram rescues him, he meets Melchizedek, and in chapter 15 God speaks to Abram about his reward.

keyFigures.name: Abram
keyFigures.role: Rescues Lot, honors Melchizedek, and refuses the king of Sodom's riches.

keyFigures.name: Lot
keyFigures.role: Captured when the eastern kings raid Sodom.

keyFigures.name: Melchizedek
keyFigures.role: King of Salem and "the priest of the most high God," who blesses Abram.

keyFigures.name: The king of Sodom
keyFigures.role: Offers Abram the goods taken in battle.

keyFigures.name: Chedorlaomer and his allies
keyFigures.role: Four eastern kings whose raid carries Lot away.

keyThemes.explanation: Abram risks his life to rescue his nephew.
Melchizedek blesses God for handing Abram's enemies over to him.
Abram gives Melchizedek a tenth of everything.
Abram refuses Sodom's riches so no one can say a king made him rich.

Genesis 15.summary: God reassures Abram after these events, promising protection and reward. Abram protests that he remains childless, and God promises him descendants as numerous as the stars; Abram believes God, and it is counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:1–6). God again promises the land. Abram prepares divided animals, and during a deep sleep he hears that his offspring will be strangers and oppressed before returning. A smoking fire pot and flaming torch pass between the pieces as God makes a covenant specifying a broad land promise (Genesis 15:7–21).
Genesis 15.whereWeAre: Abram has just won a battle and turned down a king's riches. But he still has no son, and God's promises depend on one. In this chapter God makes a formal covenant with him, and in chapter 16 Sarai tries to solve the problem her own way.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Promises Abram a son, children like the stars, and the land, and seals it with a covenant.

keyFigures.name: Abram
keyFigures.role: Asks how God's promise can come true, then believes him.

keyThemes.explanation: Abram believes God, and God counts it to him as righteousness.
Only the fire of God's presence passes between the pieces. God alone makes the promise.
God tells Abram his family will suffer as strangers for four hundred years before coming home.
God names the land he will give to Abram's children.

explainedReferences.explanation: The promise that Abraham's descendants would be numerous.
Abraham's belief being counted as righteousness.
Abraham's faith being counted as righteousness.
Abraham believing God and it being counted as righteousness.
Prediction of the descendants' oppression and deliverance.

Genesis 16.summary: Sarai, still childless, gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram so she might obtain children through her (Genesis 16:1–3). After Hagar becomes pregnant, trouble starts; Sarai mistreats Hagar, who flees. An angel of the LORD finds her by a spring, directs her to return, and promises many descendants through her son Ishmael, whose name points to God hearing her distress (Genesis 16:4–12). Hagar names God as the one who sees her. She gives birth to Ishmael when Abram is eighty-six (Genesis 16:13–16).
Genesis 16.whereWeAre: Ten years after arriving in Canaan, Abram and Sarai still have no child. Sarai gives her servant Hagar to Abram, and Ishmael is born. Thirteen years pass before God speaks to Abram again in chapter 17.

keyFigures.name: Sarai
keyFigures.role: Gives Hagar to Abram, then treats her harshly.

keyFigures.name: Abram
keyFigures.role: Takes Hagar as a wife and lets Sarai deal with her as she pleases.

keyFigures.name: Hagar
keyFigures.role: Sarai's Egyptian servant, who runs away and is found by God.

keyFigures.name: The angel of the LORD
keyFigures.role: Finds Hagar by a spring, sends her back, and promises her many descendants.

keyThemes.explanation: Sarai and Abram try to get the promised child their own way.
Sarai treats Hagar so harshly that she runs away.
God finds Hagar in the wilderness, and she calls him "Thou God seest me."
God promises Hagar that her son will have too many descendants to count.

Genesis 17.summary: When Abram is ninety-nine, God reaffirms his covenant, changes his name to Abraham and Sarai’s to Sarah, and promises nations and kings from their descendants (Genesis 17:1–16). Circumcision is commanded as the covenant sign for males in Abraham’s household, including servants, on the eighth day for newborns. God specifically promises that Sarah will bear Isaac. Abraham asks that Ishmael live under divine blessing; God blesses Ishmael but names Isaac as the son through whom the covenant will be established. Abraham circumcises his household that day (Genesis 17:17–27).
Genesis 17.whereWeAre: Thirteen years have passed since Ishmael was born. Now God appears to Abram, gives him a new name, and promises that Sarai herself will have a son. That son, Isaac, is born in chapter 21.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Gives Abram a new name, renews his covenant, and gives circumcision as its sign.

keyFigures.name: Abraham
keyFigures.role: Falls on his face before God and circumcises his whole household.

keyFigures.name: Sarah
keyFigures.role: Given a new name and the promise that she will have a son.

keyFigures.name: Ishmael
keyFigures.role: Abraham's thirteen-year-old son, blessed by God and circumcised with his father.

keyThemes.explanation: Abram becomes Abraham, "a father of many nations," and Sarai becomes Sarah.
Every male in Abraham's household is circumcised as a mark of belonging to God.
God promises a son to a man of a hundred and a woman of ninety.
God blesses Ishmael but makes his covenant with Isaac.

explainedReferences.explanation: Declaration making Abraham father of many nations.

Genesis 18.summary: The LORD appears to Abraham near the oaks of Mamre as three visitors approach; Abraham offers generous hospitality (Genesis 18:1–8). A visitor announces that Sarah will have a son, and Sarah laughs in disbelief; the LORD asks whether anything is too hard for him (Genesis 18:9–15). God reveals concern over the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah. Abraham intercedes, repeatedly asking whether the Judge of all the earth will spare the city for the sake of righteous people, reducing the proposed number to ten (Genesis 18:16–33).
Genesis 18.whereWeAre: In chapter 17 God promised Abraham that Sarah would have a son within a year. Now three visitors come and repeat that promise where Sarah can hear it. Then the LORD tells Abraham what he plans for Sodom, which leads into chapter 19.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Visits Abraham, promises Sarah a son, and tells Abraham his plan for Sodom.

keyFigures.name: Abraham
keyFigures.role: Welcomes the three visitors and pleads with the LORD for Sodom.

keyFigures.name: Sarah
keyFigures.role: Laughs when she overhears that she will have a son.

keyFigures.name: The three visitors
keyFigures.role: Men who come to Abraham's tent as the LORD appears to him.

keyThemes.explanation: Abraham hurries to serve his guests with water, bread, and a calf.
When Sarah laughs, the LORD asks, "Is any thing too hard for the LORD?"
Abraham pleads for Sodom, asking, "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?"
The cry against Sodom is great, and the LORD goes down to see it for himself.

explainedReferences.explanation: The promise that Sarah would have a son.

Genesis 19.summary: Two angels arrive at Sodom, where Lot hosts them. A mob surrounds his house and demands to assault the visitors. The angels protect the household and warn Lot to flee (Genesis 19:1–17). Lot hesitates but is led out; Sodom and Gomorrah are destroyed. Lot’s wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:18–29). Lot then lives in a cave with his daughters, who make him drunk and conceive sons, Moab and Benammi, ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites (Genesis 19:30–38).
Genesis 19.whereWeAre: Chapter 18 ended with Abraham praying for Sodom. Now two angels arrive and find the city as wicked as its outcry. Lot's family is rescued, and chapter 20 returns to Abraham.

keyFigures.name: Lot
keyFigures.role: Takes in the two angels, tries to protect them, and is led out of Sodom.

keyFigures.name: The two angels
keyFigures.role: Strike the mob blind and lead Lot's family out of the city.

keyFigures.name: The men of Sodom
keyFigures.role: Surround Lot's house and try to attack his guests.

keyFigures.name: Lot's wife
keyFigures.role: Looks back at the burning city and becomes a pillar of salt.

keyFigures.name: Lot's daughters
keyFigures.role: Make their father drunk and become the mothers of Moab and Benammi.

keyThemes.explanation: The mob shows how wicked the city is, and fire falls from heaven.
Lot lingers, but the angels take him by the hand and lead him out, "the LORD being merciful unto him."
Lot's wife disobeys the warning and becomes a pillar of salt.
Even after the rescue, Lot's family falls into shameful sin.

Genesis 20.summary: Abraham stays in Gerar and again says Sarah is his sister. Abimelech takes Sarah, but God warns him in a dream that she is married (Genesis 20:1–7). Abimelech protests his innocence and returns Sarah, rebuking Abraham for putting his household at risk. Abraham explains his fear and says Sarah is his half-sister (Genesis 20:8–13). Abimelech provides gifts, and Abraham prays; God heals the women of Abimelech’s household, whose wombs had been closed (Genesis 20:14–18).
Genesis 20.whereWeAre: Isaac's birth was promised for "this set time in the next year" (Genesis 17:21), so it is very close. Yet Abraham repeats the same lie he told in Egypt in chapter 12, and Sarah is taken again. God steps in, and in chapter 21 Isaac is finally born.

keyFigures.name: Abraham
keyFigures.role: Lies again that Sarah is his sister, then prays for Abimelech's household.

keyFigures.name: Sarah
keyFigures.role: Taken into Abimelech's house and returned untouched.

keyFigures.name: Abimelech

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Protects Sarah and heals Abimelech's household after Abraham prays.

keyThemes.explanation: Abraham repeats the lie he told in Egypt years before.
God warns Abimelech before he can touch Sarah.
Abimelech pleads his innocence and asks Abraham why he lied.
Abraham prays, and God heals Abimelech's household.

Genesis 21.summary: God fulfills the promise to Sarah, and Isaac is born; Abraham circumcises him on the eighth day. Sarah celebrates the unexpected joy (Genesis 21:1–7). Later Sarah demands that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away. Abraham is distressed, but God promises to care for Ishmael; in the wilderness Hagar despairs, God hears the boy, and they survive (Genesis 21:8–21). Abraham also resolves a dispute over a well with Abimelech, making an oath at Beersheba and calling on the LORD (Genesis 21:22–34).
Genesis 21.whereWeAre: Twenty-five years after God first called Abram, the promised son is finally born. Isaac's birth leads to Hagar and Ishmael being sent away. Next, in chapter 22, God tests Abraham with the son he waited for so long.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Gives Sarah her son and hears Ishmael crying in the desert.

keyFigures.name: Sarah
keyFigures.role: Gives birth to Isaac and asks Abraham to send Hagar and Ishmael away.

keyFigures.name: Abraham
keyFigures.role: Circumcises Isaac, sends Hagar away, and makes a treaty at Beersheba.

keyFigures.name: Hagar and Ishmael
keyFigures.role: Sent into the wilderness, where God saves them.

keyFigures.name: Abimelech and Phichol
keyFigures.role: The king of Gerar and the captain of his army, who make a treaty with Abraham.

keyThemes.explanation: Isaac is born at the very time God said.
In the desert, God hears the boy crying and shows Hagar a well.
Sending Hagar and Ishmael away grieves Abraham deeply.
Abraham and Abimelech settle a quarrel over a well with an oath.

explainedReferences.explanation: Sarah's demand to cast out the bondwoman and her son.
The promise concerning Isaac's descendants.
The promise that Abraham's seed would be named through Isaac.

Genesis 22.summary: God tests Abraham by commanding him to offer Isaac in the land of Moriah. Abraham takes Isaac, builds an altar, and prepares to act, but the angel of the LORD stops him; a ram is provided as a substitute (Genesis 22:1–14). The LORD renews promises of numerous descendants and blessing to the nations through Abraham’s offspring (Genesis 22:15–19). The chapter ends with a notice about Nahor’s family, including Rebekah, who will appear in Isaac’s story (Genesis 22:20–24).
Genesis 22.whereWeAre: Abraham waited 25 years for the son God promised, and Isaac was finally born in chapter 21. Now God asks Abraham to give him back. The chapter ends by naming Rebekah, who becomes Isaac's wife in chapter 24.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Tests Abraham, then renews his promise.

keyFigures.name: Abraham
keyFigures.role: Takes Isaac to Moriah and is ready to offer him.

keyFigures.name: Isaac
keyFigures.role: Carries the wood and asks where the lamb is.

keyFigures.name: The angel of the LORD
keyFigures.role: Calls from heaven to stop Abraham and repeats God's promise.

keyThemes.explanation: God asks Abraham to give up the son he waited for, and Abraham obeys.
God provides a ram in Isaac's place, and Abraham names the place Jehovahjireh.
The angel stops Abraham's hand before he can harm the boy.
Because Abraham obeyed, God promises that all nations will be blessed through his seed.

explainedReferences.explanation: Hebrews reproduces God's sworn blessing to Abraham.
Promise to Abraham that all families of the earth would be blessed through his seed.
The promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed through him.

Genesis 23.summary: Sarah dies at 127 in Kirjatharba, which is Hebron, and Abraham mourns her (Genesis 23:1–2). Though he is a resident foreigner, he negotiates with the Hittites for a burial site. Ephron offers the cave of Machpelah and its field, and Abraham pays the stated price before witnesses at the city gate (Genesis 23:3–18). He buries Sarah there (Genesis 23:19–20). The purchase gives Abraham his first piece of the promised land, a family grave, while the rest of the promise is still to come.
Genesis 23.whereWeAre: Years have passed since Abraham's test on Mount Moriah, and now Sarah dies. Abraham owns no land in Canaan, so he must buy a place to bury her. With Sarah gone, chapter 24 turns to finding a wife for Isaac.

keyFigures.name: Sarah
keyFigures.role: Dies at 127 in Hebron.

keyFigures.name: Abraham
keyFigures.role: Mourns Sarah and buys a cave to bury her.

keyFigures.name: Ephron
keyFigures.role: The Hittite who sells Abraham the cave and field.

keyFigures.name: The Hittites (sons of Heth)
keyFigures.role: The townspeople who witness the sale at the city gate.

keyThemes.explanation: Abraham mourns and weeps for Sarah.
Abraham calls himself "a stranger and a sojourner" in the land God promised him.
Abraham pays the full price in front of witnesses.

keyThemes.theme: A first piece of the promise
keyThemes.explanation: The cave becomes the family's first land in Canaan.

Genesis 24.summary: Abraham sends his senior servant to his relatives to find a wife for Isaac, insisting that Isaac remain in Canaan (Genesis 24:1–9). At a well the servant prays for guidance, and Rebekah offers water to him and his camels (Genesis 24:10–27). The servant recounts his mission to her family, who consent to the marriage; Rebekah herself agrees to go (Genesis 24:28–61). Isaac meets her, takes her as his wife, and is comforted after his mother’s death (Genesis 24:62–67).
Genesis 24.whereWeAre: Sarah has died, and Isaac is still unmarried. Abraham, now very old, sends his servant back to his relatives to find Isaac a wife. The chapter ends with Isaac and Rebekah married, ready for the next generation in chapter 25.

keyFigures.name: Abraham
keyFigures.role: Sends his servant to find a wife for Isaac from his own family.

keyFigures.name: Abraham's servant
keyFigures.role: Prays for guidance, finds Rebekah, and brings her home.

keyFigures.name: Rebekah
keyFigures.role: Waters the servant's camels and agrees to go and marry Isaac.

keyFigures.name: Laban and Bethuel
keyFigures.role: Rebekah's brother and father, who agree to the marriage.

keyFigures.name: Isaac
keyFigures.role: Marries Rebekah and loves her.

keyThemes.explanation: The servant prays for a sign, and God answers before he finishes praying.
Rebekah gives water not only to the servant but to all ten of his camels.
Rebekah's family asks her, and she says, "I will go."
Isaac's marriage carries God's promise into the next generation.

Genesis 25.summary: Abraham has additional descendants through Keturah, but gives his main inheritance to Isaac; he dies and is buried by Isaac and Ishmael (Genesis 25:1–11). Ishmael’s descendants are listed (Genesis 25:12–18). Rebekah struggles with infertility, and Isaac prays; she conceives twins and receives an oracle about two peoples (Genesis 25:19–23). Esau is born before Jacob. As they grow, Esau trades his birthright to Jacob for food, treating it with contempt (Genesis 25:24–34).
Genesis 25.whereWeAre: Abraham's story ends here with his death. Isaac and Rebekah, married in chapter 24, wait twenty years for children, and then twins are born. The rivalry between Jacob and Esau drives the story through chapter 33.

keyFigures.name: Abraham
keyFigures.role: Leaves everything to Isaac and dies at 175.

keyFigures.name: Ishmael
keyFigures.role: Helps Isaac bury their father. His twelve sons are listed.

keyFigures.name: Isaac
keyFigures.role: Prays for his wife, who has no children.

keyFigures.name: Rebekah
keyFigures.role: Gives birth to twins after God tells her two nations are in her womb.

keyFigures.name: Esau
keyFigures.role: The firstborn twin, who sells his birthright for stew.

keyFigures.name: Jacob
keyFigures.role: The younger twin, who buys the birthright.

keyThemes.explanation: The story passes from Abraham to Isaac and his twin sons.
Like Sarah, Rebekah cannot have children until Isaac prays for her.
Before the twins are born, God says "the elder shall serve the younger."
Esau trades his birthright for a bowl of stew. "Thus Esau despised his birthright."

Genesis 26.summary: A famine leads Isaac to Gerar, where God tells him to remain and renews promises made to Abraham (Genesis 26:1–6). Isaac presents Rebekah as his sister out of fear, but Abimelech discovers their marriage and warns his people not to harm them (Genesis 26:7–11). Isaac prospers; disputes over wells with local herders lead him to move until he finds uncontested water (Genesis 26:12–22). God appears at Beersheba, and Isaac builds an altar. Abimelech makes a peace agreement with Isaac. The chapter ends by reporting Esau’s marriages, which grieve his parents (Genesis 26:23–35).
Genesis 26.whereWeAre: Abraham has died, and this is the main chapter about Isaac as head of the family. Much of it echoes his father's life: a famine, a lie about his wife, and arguments over wells. In chapter 27 the story shifts to Isaac's sons.

keyFigures.name: Isaac
keyFigures.role: Stays in Gerar, lies about Rebekah, digs wells, and makes peace with Abimelech.

keyFigures.name: Rebekah
keyFigures.role: Isaac's wife, put at risk by his lie.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Gives Isaac the promise he made to Abraham.

keyFigures.name: Abimelech
keyFigures.role: King of the Philistines in Gerar, who uncovers the lie and later makes a treaty.

keyFigures.name: Esau
keyFigures.role: Marries two Hittite women, which grieves his parents.

keyThemes.explanation: God gives Isaac the same promise he gave Abraham.
Isaac tells the same lie about his wife that his father told.
Isaac keeps moving rather than fighting over wells, until "the LORD hath made room for us."
At Beersheba God tells Isaac not to fear, and Isaac builds an altar.

Genesis 27.summary: Aging Isaac prepares to bless Esau and sends him to hunt food. Rebekah overhears and arranges for Jacob to impersonate Esau using food, clothing, and goatskins (Genesis 27:1–17). Isaac is deceived and pronounces a blessing over Jacob. When Esau returns, the deception is uncovered, and Esau weeps and receives a different pronouncement (Genesis 27:18–40). Esau plans to kill Jacob, so Rebekah urges Jacob to go to her brother Laban; she raises concern with Isaac about local marriages (Genesis 27:41–46).
Genesis 27.whereWeAre: Isaac is old and blind, and the rivalry between Jacob and Esau that started in chapter 25 comes to a head. Jacob tricks his father and steals Esau's blessing. Esau wants to kill him, so in chapter 28 Jacob runs away from home.

keyFigures.name: Isaac
keyFigures.role: Old and blind, he plans to bless Esau but blesses Jacob instead.

keyFigures.name: Rebekah
keyFigures.role: Plans the trick, then sends Jacob away to save his life.

keyFigures.name: Jacob
keyFigures.role: Pretends to be Esau and steals his blessing.

keyFigures.name: Esau
keyFigures.role: Loses the blessing and plans to kill his brother.

keyThemes.explanation: The trick works, but it tears the family apart.
Once Isaac speaks the blessing, it cannot be taken back.
Isaac favors Esau and Rebekah favors Jacob, and both sons suffer for it.
Esau's anger forces Jacob to flee.

Genesis 28.summary: Isaac directs Jacob to seek a wife among his mother’s relatives and blesses him with the promise associated with Abraham (Genesis 28:1–5). Esau responds to his parents’ displeasure by marrying a daughter of Ishmael (Genesis 28:6–9). On his journey Jacob dreams of a stairway reaching heaven, with divine messengers and the LORD promising land, descendants, blessing to all families, and personal presence (Genesis 28:10–15). Jacob awakens in awe, names the place Bethel, sets up a stone pillar, and makes a vow (Genesis 28:16–22).
Genesis 28.whereWeAre: Jacob has just stolen Esau's blessing and is running for his life. On his first night away from home, alone and afraid, God meets him in a dream. In chapter 29 Jacob reaches his uncle Laban's home in Haran.

keyFigures.name: Isaac
keyFigures.role: Blesses Jacob and sends him to find a wife among his mother's family.

keyFigures.name: Jacob
keyFigures.role: Dreams of a ladder to heaven and makes a vow to God.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Stands above the ladder and promises to be with Jacob.

keyFigures.name: Esau
keyFigures.role: Marries a daughter of Ishmael to please his father.

keyFigures.name: The angels of God
keyFigures.role: Seen going up and down the ladder in Jacob's dream.

keyThemes.explanation: God promises, "I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest."
God gives Jacob the promise of land, children, and blessing first given to Abraham.
Jacob realizes God is in this place and names it Bethel.
Jacob vows that if God keeps him safe, the LORD will be his God.

Genesis 29.summary: Jacob arrives near Haran and meets Rachel at a well (Genesis 29:1–14). He offers to work seven years for her father Laban in exchange for marriage, but Laban deceives him into marrying Leah first. Jacob then marries Rachel, agreeing to another seven years of service (Genesis 29:15–30). Jacob loves Rachel more, while Leah is unloved. God sees Leah’s situation, and she bears Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah, naming them in ways that voice her longing and eventual praise (Genesis 29:31–35).
Genesis 29.whereWeAre: Jacob has fled from Esau and reaches Haran, the home of his mother's family. He falls in love with Rachel and works seven years for her. The trickster gets tricked, and the rivalry between Leah and Rachel carries into chapter 30.

keyFigures.name: Jacob
keyFigures.role: Works fourteen years for Laban and marries Leah and Rachel.

keyFigures.name: Rachel
keyFigures.role: Laban's younger daughter, whom Jacob loves.

keyFigures.name: Leah
keyFigures.role: Laban's older daughter, unloved by Jacob, who has four sons.

keyFigures.name: Laban
keyFigures.role: Jacob's uncle, who tricks him on his wedding night.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Sees that Leah is unloved and gives her children.

keyThemes.explanation: Jacob, who deceived his father, is now deceived by his uncle.
Jacob loves Rachel more than Leah, and the whole family suffers.
The LORD sees that Leah is unloved and gives her sons.
Leah names her fourth son Judah, saying, "Now will I praise the LORD."

Genesis 30.summary: Rachel envies Leah’s children and gives Jacob her servant Bilhah, who bears Dan and Naphtali. Leah gives her servant Zilpah, who bears Gad and Asher. Leah then bears Issachar, Zebulun, and Dinah. God remembers Rachel, and she bears Joseph (Genesis 30:1–24). Jacob negotiates compensation with Laban involving marked and speckled animals and builds up large flocks by careful breeding (Genesis 30:25–43). The chapter is full of rivalry, longing for children, and tension over wages.
Genesis 30.whereWeAre: Jacob now has two wives, and chapter 29 ended with Leah having four sons while Rachel had none. The sisters compete for children, and most of the twelve tribes of Israel are born here. Jacob grows rich, which leads to his break with Laban in chapter 31.

keyFigures.name: Rachel
keyFigures.role: Envies her sister, gives Jacob her servant, and at last has Joseph.

keyFigures.name: Leah
keyFigures.role: Has more sons and a daughter, Dinah.

keyFigures.name: Bilhah and Zilpah
keyFigures.role: The servants of Rachel and Leah, who bear four of Jacob's sons.

keyFigures.name: Jacob
keyFigures.role: Has eleven sons and a daughter and builds large flocks.

keyFigures.name: Laban
keyFigures.role: Jacob's uncle, who agrees to pay him with spotted and speckled animals.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Remembers Rachel and lets her have a child.

keyThemes.explanation: Rachel and Leah compete for children and for Jacob's love.
Rachel finally has a son when "God remembered Rachel."
The sisters give their servants to Jacob as wives in their contest for children.
Jacob's flocks grow large, even while Laban tries to cheat him.

Genesis 31.summary: God tells Jacob to return to his ancestral land. Jacob explains Laban’s changing wages to Rachel and Leah, who agree to leave (Genesis 31:1–16). While Laban is away, the household departs; Rachel steals Laban’s household gods. Laban pursues them but receives a divine warning not to threaten Jacob (Genesis 31:17–29). The confrontation includes Laban’s search for the idols, Jacob’s defense of his labor, and a covenant marked by a heap and pillar. They swear not to harm each other and part (Genesis 31:30–55).
Genesis 31.whereWeAre: Jacob has worked twenty years for Laban and become rich, and Laban's sons are angry. God tells Jacob to go home. Jacob escapes, makes peace with Laban, and in chapter 32 turns to face the brother he ran from.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Tells Jacob to go home and warns Laban in a dream.

keyFigures.name: Jacob
keyFigures.role: Leaves Laban secretly and stands up to him when he catches up.

keyFigures.name: Rachel
keyFigures.role: Steals her father's household idols and hides them.

keyFigures.name: Leah
keyFigures.role: Agrees with Rachel to leave their father.

keyFigures.name: Laban
keyFigures.role: Chases Jacob, searches for his idols, and makes a treaty with him.

keyThemes.explanation: God tells Jacob to return to the land of his fathers.
Laban changed Jacob's wages again and again, but God protected him.
Rachel's theft shows that idols still have a hold on Jacob's family.
Jacob and Laban set up a heap of stones and promise not to harm each other.

Genesis 32.summary: Jacob continues toward home and encounters angels, calling the place Mahanaim (Genesis 32:1–2). Fearing Esau’s approach with four hundred men, he sends messengers, divides his camp, prays for deliverance, and sends gifts ahead (Genesis 32:3–21). Left alone, Jacob wrestles with a man until dawn; he is wounded at the hip, receives the name Israel, and calls the place Peniel because he says he has seen God face to face (Genesis 32:22–32). The chapter mixes Jacob’s fear with prayer and a strange meeting that changes him.
Genesis 32.whereWeAre: Jacob has left Laban for good, but ahead of him is Esau, the brother who wanted to kill him twenty years ago. He hears Esau is coming with four hundred men. The night before they meet, Jacob wrestles until dawn, and in chapter 33 the brothers finally face each other.

keyFigures.name: Jacob (Israel)
keyFigures.role: Prays for help, wrestles until dawn, and is given the name Israel.

keyFigures.name: Esau
keyFigures.role: Comes to meet Jacob with four hundred men.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Hears Jacob's prayer. Jacob says he has seen God face to face.

keyFigures.name: The man who wrestles Jacob
keyFigures.role: Wrestles with him all night, touches his hip, and blesses him with a new name.

keyFigures.name: The angels of God
keyFigures.role: Meet Jacob as he travels home.

keyThemes.explanation: Afraid of Esau, Jacob prays, "I am not worthy of the least of all the mercies."
Jacob sends hundreds of animals ahead to calm his brother.
Jacob wrestles, is wounded, and is renamed Israel.
Jacob's plans cannot save him, so he clings to God and will not let go.

Genesis 33.summary: Jacob meets Esau, bowing repeatedly as he approaches. Instead of attacking, Esau runs to embrace him, and the brothers weep (Genesis 33:1–4). Jacob introduces his family and urges Esau to accept gifts. Esau offers to travel together, but Jacob declines and proceeds at a different pace (Genesis 33:5–17). Jacob reaches Shechem in Canaan, buys land, pitches his tent, and builds an altar named Elelohe-Israel (Genesis 33:18–20).
Genesis 33.whereWeAre: After a night of wrestling in chapter 32, Jacob limps out to meet Esau. Instead of the attack he feared, Esau runs to hug him. Jacob then settles near Shechem, where the tragedy of chapter 34 happens.

keyFigures.name: Jacob
keyFigures.role: Bows before Esau, gives him gifts, and settles near Shechem.

keyFigures.name: Esau
keyFigures.role: Runs to hug Jacob and forgives him.

keyFigures.name: Leah, Rachel, and the children
keyFigures.role: Come forward and bow to Esau.

keyThemes.explanation: Esau runs to meet Jacob, and they weep together.
Jacob bows seven times and calls himself Esau's servant.
Esau accepts Jacob's gift, a sign that the old wrong is forgiven.
Jacob buys land near Shechem and builds an altar.

Genesis 34.summary: Dinah, daughter of Leah and Jacob, is sexually violated by Shechem, son of Hamor, and Shechem asks to marry her (Genesis 34:1–4). Hamor and Shechem seek an agreement between their people and Jacob’s family. Jacob’s sons deceitfully demand circumcision of all local males as a condition (Genesis 34:5–24). While the men are recovering, Simeon and Levi kill the males and take Dinah; the other brothers plunder the city and take captives. Jacob rebukes his sons for jeopardizing the family, while they defend Dinah’s honor (Genesis 34:25–31).
Genesis 34.whereWeAre: Jacob has just settled near the city of Shechem. His daughter Dinah is attacked there, and her brothers take a brutal revenge. The danger this creates is why God sends Jacob to Bethel in chapter 35.

keyFigures.name: Dinah
keyFigures.role: Jacob's daughter, attacked by Shechem.

keyFigures.name: Shechem
keyFigures.role: A prince who rapes Dinah, then wants to marry her.

keyFigures.name: Hamor
keyFigures.role: Shechem's father, who asks for the marriage and a treaty.

keyFigures.name: Simeon and Levi
keyFigures.role: Dinah's brothers, who kill the men of the city.

keyFigures.name: Jacob
keyFigures.role: Says nothing at first, then rebukes his sons for putting the family in danger.

keyFigures.name: Jacob's other sons
keyFigures.role: Join in the trick and loot the city.

keyThemes.explanation: Shechem's attack on Dinah is called "folly in Israel."
The brothers use circumcision, the sign of God's covenant, to trap and kill.
Dinah was wronged, but her brothers' revenge is also wrong, as Jacob later says (Genesis 49:5–7).
Women, children, and flocks are taken in the looting.

Genesis 35.summary: God tells Jacob to go to Bethel, remove foreign gods from his household, and make an altar. Jacob obeys; God protects their journey (Genesis 35:1–8). At Bethel God renews Jacob’s name Israel and repeats promises of fruitfulness and land (Genesis 35:9–15). Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin and is buried near Ephrath. Reuben sleeps with Bilhah, and the twelve sons of Jacob are listed. Isaac dies at 180 and is buried by Esau and Jacob (Genesis 35:16–29).
Genesis 35.whereWeAre: After the violence at Shechem, God tells Jacob to go back to Bethel, where God first met him in chapter 28. The chapter closes several stories at once: Rachel dies, Isaac dies, and all twelve sons are listed. Then Genesis turns to Esau's family in chapter 36 and to Joseph in chapter 37.

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Sends Jacob back to Bethel and confirms the name Israel.

keyFigures.name: Jacob (Israel)
keyFigures.role: Has his household give up their idols and worships at Bethel.

keyFigures.name: Rachel
keyFigures.role: Dies giving birth to Benjamin.

keyFigures.name: Benjamin
keyFigures.role: Jacob's twelfth son, named Benoni by his mother and renamed by his father.

keyFigures.name: Reuben
keyFigures.role: Sleeps with Bilhah, his father's concubine.

keyFigures.name: Isaac and Esau
keyFigures.role: Isaac dies at 180, and Esau and Jacob bury him.

keyThemes.explanation: Before going to Bethel, Jacob's household buries its foreign gods.
God confirms Jacob's new name and promises nations and kings.
Deborah, Rachel, and Isaac die, but Benjamin is born.
Reuben's sin shows that the family still has deep problems.

Genesis 36.summary: The chapter records Esau’s wives, children, chiefs, and settlements, identifying Esau with Edom (Genesis 36:1–19). It also lists descendants of Seir the Horite, Edomite kings who ruled before any king ruled Israel, and chiefs connected to Esau (Genesis 36:20–43). The lists show Esau’s family growing into its own nation before the story turns back to Jacob’s family.
Genesis 36.whereWeAre: Esau and Jacob buried their father together at the end of chapter 35. This chapter lists Esau's family, who became the nation of Edom. It closes Esau's part in Genesis before chapter 37 turns to Jacob's son Joseph.

keyFigures.name: Esau (Edom)
keyFigures.role: Jacob's brother, who moves to mount Seir and becomes the father of the Edomites.

keyFigures.name: Esau's wives and sons
keyFigures.role: The founders of Edom's clans.

keyFigures.name: The Horites
keyFigures.role: The people who lived in Seir before Esau's family.

keyFigures.name: The kings and dukes of Edom
keyFigures.role: Rulers from Edom's early history.

keyThemes.explanation: Esau's family becomes Edom, a nation related to Israel.
Esau's sons and grandsons become clan chiefs.
Esau settles in mount Seir, and Edom becomes the name of the land.
Edom has kings long before Israel does.

Genesis 37.summary: Joseph, favored by Jacob, receives a special robe and reports dreams suggesting his family will bow to him, intensifying his brothers’ hatred (Genesis 37:1–11). Sent to check on them, he is plotted against. Reuben intends to rescue him, but the brothers strip Joseph and throw him into a pit; at Judah’s suggestion he is sold to traders headed for Egypt (Genesis 37:12–28). The brothers deceive Jacob with Joseph’s bloodied robe, and Jacob mourns. Joseph is sold in Egypt to Potiphar (Genesis 37:29–36).
Genesis 37.whereWeAre: Jacob is back in Canaan, and the story now turns to his favorite son, Joseph. Joseph's brothers hate him and sell him as a slave, and he is taken to Egypt. Chapter 38 pauses to follow Judah, and Joseph's story picks up again in chapter 39.

keyFigures.name: Joseph
keyFigures.role: Jacob's favorite son, a dreamer, sold into slavery by his brothers.

keyFigures.name: Jacob
keyFigures.role: Favors Joseph and mourns him when he thinks he is dead.

keyFigures.name: Joseph's brothers
keyFigures.role: Hate Joseph, sell him, and lie to their father.

keyFigures.name: Reuben
keyFigures.role: Tries to save Joseph from being killed.

keyFigures.name: Judah
keyFigures.role: Suggests selling Joseph instead of killing him.

keyFigures.name: The traders
keyFigures.role: Ishmeelite and Midianite traders who buy Joseph and take him to Egypt.

keyThemes.explanation: Jacob's favoritism and Joseph's dreams make his brothers hate him.
The brothers throw Joseph into a pit and sell him for twenty pieces of silver.
The brothers use Joseph's bloody coat to trick Jacob, as Jacob once tricked his own father with goatskins.
Joseph's dreams point to a future no one in the family can see yet.

Genesis 38.summary: Judah leaves his brothers and marries a Canaanite woman. His sons Er and Onan die; Onan had refused to provide offspring for his brother’s widow Tamar (Genesis 38:1–11). Judah withholds his remaining son Shelah from Tamar. Disguised, Tamar has an encounter with Judah and conceives; when she is accused of immorality, she produces Judah’s signet, cord, and staff, exposing his responsibility (Genesis 38:12–26). Judah acknowledges that she is more righteous than he in this matter. Tamar bears twins Pharez and Zarah (Genesis 38:27–30).
Genesis 38.whereWeAre: Joseph has just been sold into Egypt at the end of chapter 37. The story pauses here to follow Judah, the brother who suggested selling him. In chapter 39 it returns to Joseph in Egypt.

keyFigures.name: Judah
keyFigures.role: Breaks his promise to Tamar, then admits he was wrong.

keyFigures.name: Tamar
keyFigures.role: Judah's daughter-in-law, who disguises herself to claim what she was owed.

keyFigures.name: Er, Onan, and Shelah
keyFigures.role: Judah's sons. The LORD takes the lives of Er and Onan for their wickedness.

keyFigures.name: Hirah
keyFigures.role: Judah's Adullamite friend, who tries to deliver Judah's payment.

keyFigures.name: Pharez and Zarah
keyFigures.role: Tamar's twin sons.

Judah admits, "She hath been more righteous than I."
Pharez, born out of this troubled story, becomes an ancestor of King David (Ruth 4:18–22).

Genesis 39.summary: Joseph serves Potiphar in Egypt and prospers because the LORD is with him, becoming overseer of his master’s household (Genesis 39:1–6). Potiphar’s wife repeatedly pressures Joseph to have sex with her. He refuses, citing both his master’s trust and sin against God; when she seizes his garment, he flees (Genesis 39:7–12). She falsely accuses him, and Potiphar has Joseph imprisoned. Even in prison, the LORD is with Joseph, and the keeper entrusts him with responsibility (Genesis 39:13–23).
Genesis 39.whereWeAre: Chapter 37 ended with Joseph sold to Potiphar, an Egyptian officer, and chapter 38 followed Judah. Now the story returns to Joseph. He rises in Potiphar's house, is falsely accused, and lands in prison, where he meets two of Pharaoh's officials in chapter 40.

Potiphar's wife lies, and Joseph is punished for doing right.
In the house and in the prison, "the LORD was with Joseph."
Joseph works so well that everything is put into his hands.

Genesis 40.summary: In prison Joseph attends Pharaoh’s cupbearer and baker, who each have troubling dreams (Genesis 40:1–8). Joseph says interpretations belong to God and hears their dreams. He predicts that the cupbearer will be restored in three days but the baker executed (Genesis 40:9–19). Events unfold as Joseph explained at Pharaoh’s birthday feast. Joseph asks the cupbearer to remember his unjust detention, but the restored official forgets him (Genesis 40:20–23).
Genesis 40.whereWeAre: Joseph has been thrown into prison after a false charge in chapter 39. There he explains the dreams of Pharaoh's butler and baker. The butler forgets him, and Joseph waits two more years until chapter 41.

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh

Joseph asks the butler to remember him, but he forgets.
Both dreams come true on the third day, just as Joseph explained.

Genesis 41.summary: Two years later Pharaoh dreams of seven healthy cows consumed by thin cows and seven full ears of grain consumed by thin ears (Genesis 41:1–8). The cupbearer remembers Joseph, who credits God for interpretation and explains that seven plentiful years will be followed by seven years of famine. Joseph advises storage during abundance (Genesis 41:9–36). Pharaoh appoints Joseph over Egypt’s preparations. Joseph marries Asenath and has Manasseh and Ephraim. During famine people come to Egypt for grain (Genesis 41:37–57).
Genesis 41.whereWeAre: Joseph has waited in prison for two years since the butler forgot him. Now Pharaoh has dreams no one can explain, and the butler finally remembers. In one day Joseph goes from prisoner to ruler of Egypt, and the famine he predicts brings his brothers to him in chapter 42.

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh
keyFigures.role: Dreams of cows and grain and makes Joseph second only to himself.

keyFigures.name: Asenath

keyFigures.name: Manasseh and Ephraim

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Shows Pharaoh what he is about to do.

keyThemes.explanation: Joseph explains the dreams and gives Pharaoh a plan to store food.
In one day Joseph goes from the prison to ruling Egypt.
Joseph stores so much grain that he stops counting it.
When the famine comes, people from every land come to Egypt to buy grain.

Genesis 42.summary: Famine reaches Canaan, and Jacob sends ten sons to Egypt for grain while keeping Benjamin home (Genesis 42:1–5). The brothers bow before Joseph, now Egypt’s governor, without recognizing him. Joseph remembers his dreams, accuses them of being spies, and tests their story (Genesis 42:6–17). He keeps Simeon imprisoned and orders the rest to bring Benjamin. The brothers recall their guilt toward Joseph; Joseph secretly returns their money with the grain, causing alarm. Back home Jacob resists sending Benjamin (Genesis 42:18–38).
Genesis 42.whereWeAre: Joseph now rules Egypt, and the famine he predicted has spread to Canaan. His brothers come to buy grain and bow before him, just as his dreams in chapter 37 said they would. Joseph knows them, but they do not know him, and his testing of them runs through chapter 44.

keyFigures.name: Simeon

keyFigures.name: Reuben
keyFigures.role: Reminds his brothers that he warned them, and offers his own two sons as a pledge for Benjamin.

keyThemes.explanation: The brothers say, "We are verily guilty concerning our brother."
The brothers bow before Joseph, just as his dreams said they would.
Joseph tests whether his brothers are honest by telling them to bring Benjamin.
Jacob has lost Joseph and Simeon, and he refuses to risk Benjamin.

Genesis 43.summary: As famine continues, Judah persuades Jacob to send Benjamin with the brothers, personally guaranteeing his safety; they take gifts and double payment (Genesis 43:1–15). In Egypt Joseph sees Benjamin and orders a meal at his house. The brothers fear punishment over the returned money, but Joseph’s steward reassures them and releases Simeon (Genesis 43:16–25). Joseph asks about Jacob, privately weeps at the sight of Benjamin, and seats the brothers by age. Benjamin receives a much larger portion (Genesis 43:26–34).
Genesis 43.whereWeAre: In chapter 42 Joseph kept Simeon in Egypt and demanded that the brothers bring Benjamin. Now the food runs out, and Jacob must let Benjamin go. Joseph welcomes them with a feast, but his final test comes in chapter 44.

keyFigures.name: Judah
keyFigures.role: Promises to keep Benjamin safe and convinces his father.

keyFigures.name: Jacob
keyFigures.role: Lets Benjamin go and sends gifts for the ruler.

keyFigures.name: Benjamin

The brothers expect to be punished but are given a feast instead.
Seeing Benjamin, Joseph has to leave the room to weep.
Benjamin gets five times as much food, and Joseph watches to see whether the brothers will be jealous.

Genesis 44.summary: Joseph orders his steward to put silver back into his brothers’ bags and secretly place his silver cup in Benjamin’s bag (Genesis 44:1–5). The brothers depart but are overtaken and accused of theft. The cup is found with Benjamin, and they return in distress (Genesis 44:6–17). Judah pleads at length, explaining Jacob’s grief and his own guarantee, and offers to remain as a slave in Benjamin’s place (Genesis 44:18–34). The chapter reaches a turning point as Judah demonstrates willingness to sacrifice his freedom for his brother.
Genesis 44.whereWeAre: The brothers have eaten with Joseph and are heading home with Simeon and Benjamin. Joseph hides his silver cup in Benjamin's sack to give them one last test. Judah's answer leads Joseph to reveal himself in chapter 45.

keyThemes.explanation: Will the brothers leave Benjamin behind, as they once left Joseph?

Judah offers himself as a slave so that Benjamin can go home.
The brothers who sold Joseph now refuse to abandon Benjamin.

Genesis 45.summary: Unable to contain his emotion, Joseph dismisses his attendants and reveals himself to his brothers. They are dismayed, but he reassures them that God sent him ahead to preserve life during the famine, without denying their act of selling him (Genesis 45:1–8). Joseph tells them to bring Jacob and the household to Egypt, where he can provide for them through remaining famine years (Genesis 45:9–15). Pharaoh supports the invitation and supplies transport. The brothers return, tell Jacob Joseph is alive, and Jacob resolves to see him (Genesis 45:16–28).
Genesis 45.whereWeAre: Judah has just offered himself as a slave in Benjamin's place. Joseph can't hold back any longer and tells his brothers who he is. Then he sends for Jacob, and in chapter 46 the whole family moves to Egypt.

keyFigures.name: Joseph

keyFigures.name: Joseph's brothers

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh

keyFigures.name: Jacob

keyThemes.explanation: Joseph hugs and kisses the brothers who sold him.
Joseph says, "God did send me before you to preserve life," without pretending his brothers did no wrong.
Joseph will provide for the whole family through the five years of famine still to come.
Jacob's spirit revives when he learns that Joseph is alive.

Genesis 46.summary: Israel sets out for Egypt, stops at Beersheba to offer sacrifices, and receives God’s assurance not to fear: God will make him a great nation in Egypt and bring his descendants back (Genesis 46:1–4). Jacob’s children and descendants travel with livestock and possessions, and the chapter lists the family grouped by their mothers (Genesis 46:5–27). Judah goes ahead to Joseph, and father and son reunite in Goshen. Joseph prepares his brothers to explain their occupation as shepherds to Pharaoh (Genesis 46:28–34).
Genesis 46.whereWeAre: Jacob has just learned that Joseph is alive. Now he leaves Canaan with his whole family to move to Egypt. This move sets up the book of Exodus, where Jacob's family grows into a nation and is later rescued from slavery.

The list names everyone who goes to Egypt, the family that will become Israel.
Joseph falls on his father's neck and weeps a long time.

Genesis 47.summary: Joseph presents five brothers to Pharaoh, who permits the family to settle in Goshen; Jacob also meets and blesses Pharaoh (Genesis 47:1–12). As famine intensifies, Joseph collects payments for grain, then livestock, then land, until the farmland belongs to Pharaoh and the people give him a fifth of their harvest; only the priests keep their land (Genesis 47:13–26). Israel’s family grows in Goshen. Near death, Jacob asks Joseph to swear that he will bury him with his ancestors rather than in Egypt (Genesis 47:27–31).
Genesis 47.whereWeAre: Jacob's family has just arrived in Egypt and been reunited with Joseph. Pharaoh gives them the land of Goshen. As the famine gets worse, Joseph keeps Egypt alive, and the chapter ends with Jacob near death, which leads into his final blessings in chapters 48–49.

keyFigures.name: Jacob

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh

keyFigures.name: The people of Egypt

The people sell everything they have, until the land belongs to Pharaoh.
In Goshen, Jacob's family grows and multiplies greatly.
Jacob makes Joseph swear to bury him with his fathers.

Genesis 48.summary: As Jacob weakens, Joseph brings his sons Manasseh and Ephraim to him. Jacob recounts God’s promise at Luz and adopts the two boys as his own for inheritance purposes (Genesis 48:1–7). Though Manasseh is older, Jacob deliberately crosses his hands to place his right hand on Ephraim, blessing the younger first. Joseph objects, but Jacob insists that both will become great and that Ephraim’s offspring will be greater (Genesis 48:8–20). Jacob expresses confidence God will bring the family back to its ancestral land (Genesis 48:21–22).
Genesis 48.whereWeAre: Jacob is near death in Egypt and has made Joseph promise to bury him in Canaan. Now Joseph brings his two sons to be blessed. In chapter 49 Jacob blesses all twelve of his own sons.

keyFigures.name: Manasseh

keyThemes.explanation: Jacob passes God's promise on to his grandsons.
Jacob crosses his hands to put Ephraim ahead of Manasseh.
Jacob speaks of "the God which fed me all my life long."
Jacob tells Joseph that God will bring the family back to Canaan.

Genesis 49.summary: Jacob gathers his sons and speaks a poem about each son’s character and future, sometimes blessing and sometimes criticizing them (Genesis 49:1–27). Reuben’s instability costs him preeminence; Simeon and Levi are rebuked for violence; Judah receives images of leadership; Joseph receives expansive blessing. Other sons receive shorter sayings using animal, land, or military imagery. Jacob then instructs them to bury him in the cave of Machpelah with his ancestors, and he dies (Genesis 49:28–33).
Genesis 49.whereWeAre: Jacob has just blessed Joseph's sons in chapter 48. Now he gathers all twelve sons and speaks over each one. He dies at the end of the chapter, and Genesis closes with his burial in chapter 50.

keyFigures.name: Jacob

Jacob asks to be buried in Canaan with his fathers.

Genesis 50.summary: Joseph weeps over Jacob and orders Egyptian embalming. After official mourning, Pharaoh permits the family to take Jacob to Canaan, where they bury him at Machpelah (Genesis 50:1–14). Back in Egypt the brothers fear that Joseph may now retaliate. Joseph weeps, refuses to take God’s place as judge, and assures them that although they intended harm, God intended good to preserve many lives (Genesis 50:15–21). Joseph lives to see later generations, expresses faith that God will bring Israel out of Egypt, and asks that his bones be carried to the promised land. He dies at 110 (Genesis 50:22–26).
Genesis 50.whereWeAre: Jacob has just died after blessing his sons. Joseph buries him in Canaan, and then the brothers fear Joseph will finally take revenge. Genesis ends with Joseph's death in Egypt, and the story picks up in Exodus after Jacob's family has grown into a nation.
